title: Balanitis
subject: Pathology
summary: Inflammation of the glans penis, often extending to the foreskin. Common in uncircumcised men, especially with poor hygiene, diabetes, or Candida infection. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by simple microscopy when available.

sections.p: Balanitis is inflammation of the glans penis, with or without involvement of the prepuce (balanoposthitis). Diagnosis is made by history and visual inspection; microscopy of a swab can identify Candida or bacterial pathogens when resources allow.
b: Red, painful glans; possible swelling, discharge, or fissuring
Often associated with poor hygiene, diabetes, or recent antibiotic use
Mild: erythema, mild discomfort, no ulceration
Moderate: marked erythema, edema, fissures, discharge
Severe: extensive edema, ulceration, necrosis, or paraphimosis

sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings the most frequent causes are:
b: Candida albicans – especially in diabetics or after broad‑spectrum antibiotics
Staphylococcus aureus – common skin flora, worsened by poor hygiene
Streptococcus pyogenes – acute bacterial balanitis
Irritant dermatitis – soaps, herbal preparations
Sexually transmitted infections – HSV, syphilis, gonorrhoea (less common)

sections.p: Patients report redness, burning, itching, and sometimes a thick white discharge. In uncircumcised men the foreskin may be difficult to retract (phimosis) or become trapped (paraphimosis).
b: Painful glans, often worse after urination
Foul‑smelling or cheesy discharge if Candida
Swelling that may impede retraction of the foreskin

sections.p: When microscopy is unavailable, treat empirically based on the most likely cause (Candida or bacterial).

t.a: Wet mount microscopy of glans swab
t.b: Is the inflammation infectious? – Pseudohyphae or budding yeasts confirm Candida; Gram stain shows bacteria
Is diabetes a predisposing factor? – Elevated glucose supports Candida‑related balanitis
Does immunosuppression increase risk? – Positive result raises suspicion for atypical infections
Is there concurrent urinary infection? – Leukocyte esterase or nitrites suggest co‑existing UTI

sections.p: Complications arise from delayed treatment or severe inflammation.
b: Paraphimosis causing vascular compromise
Necrotizing ulceration (rare, usually bacterial)
Secondary infection spreading to the urethra or bloodstream
Development of lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans)

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve symptoms, and educate on hygiene.
b: Topical antifungal (clotrimazole 1% cream) for Candida – chosen for efficacy and low systemic absorption
Topical antibacterial (mupirocin) for suspected bacterial infection – avoids systemic side‑effects
Gentle retraction and cleaning with warm water; avoid soaps or irritants
Circumcision for recurrent balanitis in uncircumcised men – removes the niche for pathogens
Control diabetes or other systemic risk factors

sections.p: Re‑evaluate after 7‑10 days; ensure resolution of signs. Prevent recurrence with daily hygiene and control of diabetes.
b: Ask patient to return if pain persists or swelling worsens
Teach proper cleaning technique: retract foreskin, wash with water, dry gently
Screen for diabetes if not previously diagnosed
Lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans) – white atrophic patches, chronic course
Herpes simplex infection – vesicular lesions, systemic prodrome
Penile psoriasis – well‑demarcated plaques, silvery scale
Negative microscopy does not exclude Candida if sample is inadequate
Normal blood glucose does not rule out intermittent hyperglycaemia in diabetics

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly increasing swelling of the glans or foreskin (possible paraphimosis)
Systemic signs: fever, chills, or malaise

faq.q: Can balanitis occur in circumcised men?
faq.a: Yes, but it is far less common; when it does occur, consider irritant dermatitis or STI.

faq.q: Why is Candida the most common cause in diabetics?
faq.a: High glucose levels promote yeast growth and impair local immunity.

faq.q: Is partner treatment needed for Candida balanitis?
faq.a: Routine partner treatment is not required unless the partner has symptoms.

exam: What bedside signs differentiate Candida from bacterial balanitis? — Look for thick white discharge and itching (Candida) versus purulent exudate and acute pain (bacterial).

A patient with uncontrolled diabetes presents with painful glans erythema and white discharge. What is your next step? — Perform a wet‑mount microscopy; if unavailable, start topical antifungal while arranging glucose control.
How would you manage a case of balanitis complicated by paraphimosis? — Reduce edema manually with lubrication, give analgesia, and arrange urgent urological review for possible circumcision.

Why is circumcision recommended for recurrent balanitis in low‑resource settings? — It eliminates the moist subpreputial space that harbours pathogens, reducing recurrence without need for long‑term medication.

A patient reports using a traditional herbal paste on his penis and now has erythema and fissuring. What is the likely diagnosis and management? — Irritant dermatitis; advise cessation of the paste, gentle cleansing, and a mild topical steroid if inflammation persists.

What laboratory test would you order to assess an underlying systemic risk factor, and how would the result influence treatment? — Point‑of‑care glucose; hyperglycaemia would prompt tighter diabetic control and favours antifungal therapy.

Explain why routine partner treatment is not indicated for Candida balanitis. — Candida colonisation is usually endogenous; partners are asymptomatic and treatment offers no benefit unless they have symptoms.
Describe the key features that would make you suspect lichen sclerosus rather than acute balanitis. — Chronic white atrophic plaques, itching, and phimosis without acute discharge.
